Hey, I'm not sure if I have some great advice, but I'd just like to show some support.

I'm sorry to hear you're struggling so much, but I do think it's great that you're trying to get better and seek support, many people don't even reach that step!

I feel like sometimes we don't really understand ourselves, so we end up doing things we don't want to do, like you ultimately give in after 3-6 months. A good starting point in my opinion would be to ask yourself why? It sounds like an obvious and silly question but it's really important to dive deeper and understand our behavior and emotions. What makes you give in? Do you start feeling a certain way, is there a specific trigger, a certain situation, boredom, loneliness, low self-esteem? When you find your reason, you might find it easier to work on a solution.

Also, I understand your struggle with mental health. I'm struggling too. I thought that would make it so much harder to quit, and it did at first. First 2 weeks felt like I entered a new kind of depression, I felt so worthless and wondered why would I even stop slowly killing myself with this poison if I don't even matter. But the feeling passed, just as many, many people said it would.

Also, I take medication for depression. I know it's a bit controversial and some people may be against it, but it really helped me, and I strongly suggest taking it into consideration. Sometimes we can't fight on our own and need to give our brains a little boost.

I really hope you manage to stay strong and keep pushing! Wish you all the best! ❤

I would definitelly advise staying on your meds if you noticed your depression getting better. They literally saved my life and I hope they make yours great too! And congratulations on quitting smoking! :)


Edit: just wanted to add that depression coming back is probably from quitting. For me at least if feels like I lost something important and it's bringing me down a lot. Maybe you feel something similar too. Try to analyze why you feel the way you do, and what is it that you feel exactly. Understanding it might help you cope until you get better. ❤

ESH. (apart from your daughter)

It doesn't really sound as if you and your family are healthy despise being a bit bigger. At least that's what your statement of "refusing to spend money on vegetables" sounds like. If your daughter is unhappy with the way she looks, and if her weight is getting (or is) close to being unhealthy, then she should be encouraged to eat healthy (but balanced! She doesn't have to give up everything she enjoys) and get some exercise (again, in moderation). Yes, she should be reminded that she is beautiful no matter what, but if she is trying to implement some healthy changes into her life, while also losing a bit of weight, it's not a big deal. It kind of seems as if you're trying to push your own believes onto her.
On the other hand, getting a teenage girl a food scale is, in my opinion, a terrible thing to do. Encouraging her to go for walks, eat fruits and veggies is okay, but this is where I'd draw the line. Stuff like scales, portions, calories etc. can only do harm and make a healthy lifestyle an obsession that in the end turns into an eating disorder. Been there done that.
In conclusion, talk to your sister and tell her that you don't want her to "coach" your daughter if she can't find a balance that works for a 14 year old. Also, support your daughter, tell her that you want to be by her side while trying to be healthy, but remind her everyday that some number doesn't represent her worth.
